prize_parts.citation: for an oeuvre that renews lyric, essay and verse narrative through a dialogue with antiquity and the fragment, and that makes the hybrid book a form of intellectual and elegiac inquiry

statement.case_for: My opening view holds after reconsideration. Carson's strongest claim rests on distinctiveness of voice and on formal achievement that is also intellectual. Autobiography of Red recasts an ancient myth as a modern verse novel. Nox turns elegy, philological commentary and fragmentary material into a single work. Her long engagement with Greek and Latin texts through translation and commentary is part of the same project and is not an academic sideline. The recurring question of how a lost or broken text can still speak gives the oeuvre a continuous imaginative and intellectual centre across genres. On the criteria of voice, formal invention and depth, I find this a strong case. It is made with the caveat that my knowledge rests on public knowledge and translations of classical sources, not on independent verification.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that hybrid and book-object work is hard to weigh against more conventional oeuvres, and that the evidence for sustained depth may rest on a few celebrated books. Part of the output consists of translations, adaptations, performance texts and limited-edition formats. How much of this is her own literary achievement, and how much a citation could responsibly cover, remains unsettled. Cărtărescu offers a more unified long-form achievement in the novel, and I cannot dismiss the possibility that he is the stronger candidate on sustained quality.

responses.point: Carlberg rates Carson's formal originality and intellectual depth highly, but asks whether the oeuvre is sustained across its many hybrid experiments. She also doubts how much weight translations and the visual book-object elements can carry in a citation.
responses.response: I take the sustainability question as the real test, and I do not think it can be settled by pointing to the celebrated titles alone. My reading is that the recurring concerns are the fragment, loss and the afterlife of ancient texts, and that they give the later books a continuity beyond experimentation for its own sake. I accept that this continuity is not demonstrated by the opening evidence. On translations I agree that the citation should rest on her own poetry, verse narrative and essays, with the classical work as context. On the visual elements I would assess the text and treat the book design as a feature of how the text is composed, not as a separate criterion.

responses.point: Mattson ranks Cărtărescu first for visionary prose that joins memory, body and dream in a long, coherent project, with a late-career peak in Solenoid. She names the length and encyclopedic excess of the later books as a possible weakness for sustained quality.
responses.response: I agree that the imaginative scale and recognisable voice are real, and Cărtărescu is the strongest alternative to my own preference. I would qualify the claim that scale in itself shows sustained quality, which is the very question Mattson raises about excess. For Carson the corresponding worry is the opposite one, that concision and variety might hide a lack of depth. Neither worry is settled by the opening evidence. I would want the committee to compare how each writer's formal choices generate meaning, and not treat dimension or novelty as a measure of achievement. Her comment also shows that all of us depend on translations of dense Romanian prose, which limits my own confidence in ranking him above or below Carson.

responses.point: Palm also ranks Carson first. She describes a distinctive voice, sustained formal inventiveness and a decades-long engagement with ancient texts and with grief. She flags that the book-object works and the translations are hard to separate from the creative oeuvre for citation purposes.
responses.response: I agree with the description of the voice and with the point about citation scope, and I would not treat our shared view as evidence in itself. Her observation on separating the translations from the creative work is the more useful contribution. I would draft the citation around the renewal of lyric, essay and verse narrative and mention antiquity as the field of dialogue, so that a reader does not take the prize as a recognition of classical scholarship. Palm's remark that some later output appears in performance or limited-edition formats also keeps me cautious. It means the printed record on which a committee can base a judgement may be thinner for the recent period than for the major books.

responses.point: Sem-Sandberg ranks Cărtărescu first and Carson second. He credits Carson's hybrid works with real emotional and intellectual weight, but asks whether the body of work sustains literary depth beyond its most celebrated books, and notes that translations and adaptations complicate what counts as her own oeuvre.
responses.response: That question is fair, and I consider it the main open point in my own preference. I would answer it by asking whether the lesser-known books develop the same concerns or only vary the format, which I can judge only partially and from public knowledge. His distinction between her own oeuvre and the adaptations supports keeping the citation narrow. I would still hold that a few works of lasting formal importance, within a body that shows a consistent method, can meet the standard of an oeuvre. I do not think the standard requires volume.

uncertainties: Whether Carson's later and less celebrated books sustain the depth of Autobiography of Red and Nox. I judge this from public knowledge and not from verified reading of the whole corpus.
How much of her output (translations, adaptations, performance texts, limited-edition book objects) belongs in a citation about her own literary achievement.
Whether her influence and formal achievement extend beyond Anglophone poetry, and how her allusive, classically informed English reads in translation into other languages.

Cărtărescu's comparative standing. His achievement depends on Romanian prose that I can assess only through translation, and I cannot determine whether the scale of the later novels is sustained or excessive.
The poetry of Adonis, which I rank highly on formal and linguistic grounds, cannot be judged from outside Arabic, and I cannot assess the quality of the most recent decades.
statement.conflict_note: None apparent from the supplied profile. The profile records scholarly work on the literary fragment, exile literature and Celan, and I list it only as context. It is not evidence that I favour any candidate, and no personal or institutional link to Carson or any other shortlisted writer is documented.
